newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl starts Asian trip with visit to Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Kohl starts Asian trip with visit to Indonesia.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl will be looking to expand German business ties in Indonesia on a three-day visit starting on Saturday, but he may find human rights grabbing much of the attention.

Kohl, who will lead a delegation of 56 German industrialists to Jakarta, had his hopes of keeping the trip's focus on business dashed when the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to two East Timorese earlier this month.

Jose Ramos-Horta, an exiled campaigner for independence who shared the award with East Timor's Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo, has pointedly called upon Kohl to use his influence in Jakarta to reduce tensions in East Timor.
"No other country in Europe has the same weight, the influence on Indonesia as Germany," Ramos-Horta said after winning the award.

Indonesia has faced international criticism for sending troops into East Timor in 1975 and annexing it the following year. The United Nations still recognises Portugal, the former colonial power, as the enclave's administrative authority.
Kohl, who calls Indonesian President Suharto a "good friend of Germany", was conspicuously absent from a list of world leaders who congratulated the Nobel Prize winners.
He paid a private visit to Suharto in July when the 75-year-old Indonesian leader was having a medical check-up in a German hospital in the northern town of Bad Oeynhausen.
Kohl will be in Indonesia from October 26 to 29. He will then visit the Philippines from October 29 to 31 before spending two days in Japan.
Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres appealed to Kohl recently to use his trip to exert a positive influence on Jakarta to improve what he described as "intolerable conditions" in East Timor.
"The present situation cannot be tolerated for much longer and we are counting on our friends and allies, for example Germany, to help to change things," Guterres said.

A German government official said on Thursday Kohl would raise the issue of human rights during his trip. Even though Kohl did not have any plans to met opposition leaders himself, such contacts would be made by others in the delegation.
"Of course the chancellor will speak about human rights," the official said. "There are no subjects that are uncomfortable for him."
Suharto's 1995 trip to Germany was marked by demonstrations from human rights groups which accuse Indonesia of sacrificing human rights and environmental concerns in favour of economic growth.
Germany has in the past chided Indonesia over its human rights record, saying economic development must go hand in hand with respect for human rights.
But this has not slowed strong growth in economic ties between the two countries in recent years.

Germany is Indonesia's largest European market. Two-way trade has grown by 75 percent overall since 1990 and reached 6.8 billion marks ($4.46 billion) in 1995, said Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, who will be in the delegation.
Last year, Germany and Indonesia signed an accord to mesh their economic and technological expertise as part of a drive to increase bilateral trade.
The possibility of German participation in the production of a commuter aircraft being built by Indonesia is likely to be one of the projects discussed, officials in Jakarta said. ($1=1.5247 Mark)
